1.title: CDMP FUNDAMENTALS
1.text: Welcome to Module 5: Data Modeling and Design. This is Chapter 5 of the DMBOK, and along with Governance, Metadata, and Data Quality, it's one of the highest-weighted chapters on the exam — about eleven percent, roughly twelve questions. This is a technical, detail-rich chapter, so there are a lot of precise facts to learn: building blocks, key types, normal forms, dimensional design. The good news is that it's also one of the most logical chapters, so if you understand the concepts rather than just memorizing, the questions become very answerable. Let's begin.

1.title: Module Overview & Learning Objectives
1.text: Here's what you'll master. You'll be able to define data modeling and name its four building blocks. You'll identify entities, relationships, attributes, and domains, along with the different key types. You'll compare the six modeling schemes — relational, dimensional, and the rest. You'll work through the three levels of abstraction, conceptual to logical to physical, and the six normal forms. You'll understand dimensional design, including star versus snowflake schemas, slowly changing dimensions, and grain. And you'll be able to apply the PRISM principles, the Data Model Scorecard, and naming standards. It's a lot, but it's all connected. Let's start with the definition.

1.title: Definition & Goal
1.text: The DMBOK defines data modeling as the process of discovering, analyzing, and scoping data requirements, and then representing and communicating them in a precise form called the data model. Two words in there deserve emphasis. First, the process is iterative — you don't get it right in one pass; you refine through conceptual, logical, and physical models. Second, the output is precise — a model is an exact representation, not a sketch. The goal is to confirm and document an understanding of different perspectives, which leads to applications that align with business requirements and lays the foundation for big initiatives like Master Data Management and data governance. And here's a connecting idea: data models are themselves an important form of metadata. Good modeling lowers support costs and increases reuse.

1.title: Why Data Models Matter
1.text: Why bother modeling at all? The DMBOK gives four business drivers — four reasons models are critical. One, they provide a common vocabulary around data, so everyone means the same thing by "customer." Two, they capture and document explicit knowledge about an organization's data and systems. Three, they serve as a primary communications tool during projects. And four, they provide the starting point for customizing, integrating, or replacing an application. Beyond those, confirming perspectives delivers three values: formalization, which gives you precise structures and fewer anomalies; scope definition, which sets clear boundaries; and knowledge retention, which preserves corporate memory. If you take one theme away, let it be this: the data model is fundamentally a communication tool between business and IT. That framing shows up in several exam answers.

1.title: The 4 Types of Data That Can Be Modeled
1.text: The DMBOK identifies four types of data you can model, and it helpfully maps each to a familiar IT term. Category information classifies and assigns types — customer segments, product types. Resource information is the basic profile of operational resources like Product, Customer, and Supplier — and in IT terms, that's Reference Data. Business event information is created as operational processes run — Orders, Invoices, Withdrawals — which we usually call transactional data. And detail transaction information is the high-volume stuff from point-of-sale systems, sensors, social media, and GPS — in other words, Big Data. So the mapping to remember is: Resource equals Reference Data, Business Event equals Transactional, and Detail Transaction equals Big Data.

1.title: The 4 Building Blocks of a Data Model
1.text: Every data model, regardless of scheme, is built from four components, and you need these cold. Entities — the nouns, the things we collect information about. Relationships — the associations between those entities. Attributes — the properties that identify, describe, or measure an entity. And domains — the complete set of values an attribute is allowed to hold. Entities, relationships, attributes, domains. We'll take each one in turn over the next several slides, because the exam tests the details of all four.

1.title: Entities
1.text: An entity is a thing about which an organization collects information — essentially, the nouns of the business. A helpful way to discover entities is to ask the fundamental questions: Who, What, When, Where, Why, How, and Measurement. Who gives you Employee or Customer. What gives you Product or Service. When gives you Date or Quarter. Where gives you Address or URL. Why gives you Order or Claim. How gives you Invoice or Contract. And Measurement gives you Sales or Balance. One more useful fact: entities are called different things at different levels. At the conceptual level it's a concept or term, at the logical level it's an entity, and at the physical level it's a table — that last one, table, is the most common alias and worth remembering.

1.title: High-Quality Entity Definitions
1.text: A model is only as good as its definitions, and the DMBOK says a high-quality entity definition has three characteristics. Clarity: it's easy to read, with no obscure acronyms or ambiguous terms. Accuracy: it's precise and correct, and it's been reviewed by business experts. And completeness: all the parts are present — for example, examples for codes, or the scope of uniqueness for identifiers. Clarity, accuracy, completeness. If a question asks what makes a definition high-quality, those three words are your answer.

1.title: Relationships — Cardinality & Arity
1.text: A relationship is an association between entities — the concept comes from Chen in 1976 — and in relational databases it's implemented through foreign keys. Two properties matter. First, cardinality: how many instances of one entity relate to how many of another. The options on each side are zero, one, or many. Second, arity: how many entities participate in the relationship. A unary relationship, also called recursive, involves a single entity referencing itself — and if it's one-to-many it forms a hierarchy, while many-to-many forms a network. A binary relationship involves two entities, and it's the most common type you'll see. A ternary relationship involves three. The exam favorite here is the recursive relationship — for example, an employee who reports to another employee. That's one entity relating to itself: unary.

1.title: Identifying vs. Non-Identifying Relationships
1.text: Now some finer distinctions. An independent entity has a primary key made up only of its own attributes, and it's drawn as a plain rectangle. A dependent entity has a primary key that includes at least one attribute borrowed from another entity, and it's drawn as a rounded rectangle. Related to this: in an identifying relationship, the parent's primary key migrates into the child's own primary key. In a non-identifying relationship, the parent's primary key migrates as just a regular, non-key foreign key. And the most important construct here is the associative entity — it resolves a many-to-many relationship and holds the attributes that belong to the relationship itself, like an ORDERLINE between Order and Product. Remember that: you resolve many-to-many relationships with an associative entity that carries the shared attributes.

1.title: Attributes & Keys by Construction
1.text: An attribute is a property that identifies, describes, or measures an entity; physically it's a column or field. Now let's talk keys, because the exam tests them precisely. First, keys by construction. A simple key is a single attribute that uniquely identifies an instance — a UPC or a VIN. A surrogate key is a system-generated integer with no business meaning, not visible to users, used purely for technical purposes. A compound key is two or more attributes that together identify an instance. And a composite key contains a compound key plus at least one additional attribute. The most tested of these is the surrogate key: it's stable, system-generated, and has no business meaning — and importantly, surrogate keys and business keys are mutually exclusive. You use one or the other, not both, as your identifier.

1.title: Keys by Function
1.text: Keys can also be classified by function, and there's a nice narrowing logic to them. A super key is any set of attributes that uniquely identifies an instance — it might include extra, unnecessary attributes. A candidate key is the minimal such set — no subset of it can still uniquely identify, so there's nothing extra. The primary key is the one candidate key you choose to be the official identifier. An alternate key is a candidate key you didn't choose, but it can still find specific instances. And a business key, or natural key, is the attribute or attributes a business person would actually use to look something up. The progression to remember: super key is any, candidate key is minimal, primary key is chosen. That narrowing often appears in exam questions.

1.title: Domains — 5 Ways to Define Valid Values
1.text: The fourth building block is the domain — the complete set of possible values an attribute can be assigned. The DMBOK gives five ways to define a domain. By data type, like integer, character of length thirty, or date. By data format, using templates or masks, like a postal code or phone number pattern. By a list, a finite set of allowed values such as Open, Shipped, Closed, Returned. By a range, all values between a minimum and a maximum. And by a rule, where values must satisfy a condition — for instance, item price must be greater than item cost. Domains enforce valid values, and the same domain can be reused across many attributes, which is part of why they're a distinct building block.

1.title: The 6 Modeling Schemes
1.text: The DMBOK describes six modeling schemes, and you should be able to recognize each one's signature. Relational, with notations like IE, IDEF1X, Barker, and Chen, traces back to Codd in 1970. Dimensional, the star and snowflake world, came from General Mills and Dartmouth in the 1960s. Object-oriented uses the UML class diagram. Fact-based modeling, like ORM, was formalized by Halpin in 1989. Time-based includes Data Vault and Anchor Modeling. And NoSQL covers document, key-value, column, and graph stores. The signatures to memorize: relational means "one fact in one place"; dimensional means fact tables plus dimension tables; and object-oriented uniquely adds operations, or methods, which entity-relationship models don't have. We'll go through the important ones in detail next.

1.title: The Relational Scheme
1.text: The relational scheme was originated by Dr. Edward Codd in 1970, and it's the foundation of most operational databases. It has two design objectives, both testable. First, the exact expression of business data. Second — and this is the famous one — one fact in one place, which means removing redundancy so that each piece of data lives in exactly one location. The most common notation for relational models is IE, Information Engineering notation, which uses the distinctive "crow's feet" or tridents to depict cardinality. Relational modeling is ideal for operational systems, where you need fast, accurate data entry and storage. So anchor these facts: Codd, 1970, "one fact in one place," and crow's-foot IE notation.

1.title: The Dimensional Scheme
1.text: The dimensional scheme is optimized not for data entry but for query and analysis — it's the world of data warehousing. It has two kinds of tables. Fact tables hold the numeric measurements; they have enormous row counts and take up roughly ninety percent of the database space. Dimension tables hold the textual descriptors you "query by" or "report by"; they're the primary source for slicing data, they make up only about ten percent of the space, and they're highly denormalized. A crucial concept is the grain — the meaning or description of a single row in a fact table. Defining the grain is one of the key steps in dimensional design. Finally, conformed dimensions and facts are built for the entire organization so they can be shared across multiple dimensional models with consistent terminology. Remember the ninety-ten split, and remember that grain equals the meaning of one fact-table row.

1.title: Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD)
1.text: Dimension attributes change over time — a customer moves, a product gets recategorized — and slowly changing dimensions, or SCDs, are how we handle that. There are three types — the three cards on screen — and a great mnemonic is ORC: Overwrite, Row, Column. Type 1, Overwrite, simply replaces the old value with the new one in place — you lose the history. Type 2, New Row, adds a brand-new row with the new values and marks the old row as no longer current — this preserves full history and is the most common for tracking change over time. Type 3, New Column, keeps multiple values in separate columns on the same row, letting you see, say, the current and previous value side by side. ORC — Overwrite, Row, Column — maps to Types 1, 2, and 3.

1.title: Star vs. Snowflake
1.text: Two dimensional schema shapes, shown side by side on screen, and the exam loves to contrast them. In a star schema, the dimensions are collapsed — that is, denormalized — into a single table per dimension. This keeps the design simple and queries fast, which is why star schemas are so popular. In a snowflake schema, the dimensions are not collapsed; they stay normalized, broken out into hierarchical sub-tables, which is where the snowflake shape comes from. In fact, the act of normalizing a star dimension is literally called snowflaking. So the one-line distinction to lock in: star schema means denormalized dimensions, snowflake means normalized dimensions. Don't let the exam flip those on you.

1.title: Object-Oriented & Fact-Based Schemes
1.text: Two more schemes. Object-oriented modeling uses the UML class diagram, and its defining feature is that a class has not just attributes but also operations, or methods — the behaviors. That's the thing entity-relationship models don't capture. Fact-based modeling, which includes Object-Role Modeling, ORM, and FCO-IM, is quite different. Terry Halpin formalized ORM as first-order logic in 1989. Its hallmark is that it has no attributes at all — everything is expressed as a fact type, and entities and attributes are derived from those facts rather than defined upfront. It also uses natural-language verbalization, so you can read the model almost like sentences. So two contrasts to remember: object-oriented adds operations, and ORM has no attributes and reads in natural language.

1.title: Time-Based Schemes
1.text: Time-based schemes are designed to handle history and change, and there are two you should know by their components. Data Vault has three entity types: hubs, which represent the primary keys or main business concepts; links, which integrate transactions between hubs; and satellites, which hold the descriptive context and support varying types of history. Anchor Modeling has four concepts: anchors, which model entities and events; attributes, which model properties of anchors; ties, which model relationships between anchors; and knots, which model shared properties like states. So remember: Data Vault is hubs, links, and satellites; Anchor Modeling is anchors, attributes, ties, and knots.

1.title: The NoSQL Scheme
1.text: The sixth scheme is NoSQL, and there are four types to know. A document store holds a complete business subject within a single document structure. A key-value store has just two columns — a key and a value, where the value can hold anything from a simple number to a complex object. A column-oriented store is the closest to a traditional relational database, but it stores each column in its own structure and handles complex data types well. And a graph database is best when your data's relationships are naturally represented as nodes with undetermined, flexible connections. One important note: NoSQL modeling is a physical-only technique — you model at the physical level, not conceptual or logical. Four types: document, key-value, column-oriented, and graph.

1.title: Three Levels of Detail — ANSI/SPARC (1975)
1.text: Now one of the most important frameworks in the chapter: the three levels of model detail you see on screen, which trace back to the ANSI/SPARC three-schema approach of 1975. The conceptual data model, the CDM, is requirements planning — it's high-level, capturing the critical entities, their relationships, the scope, and key terminology, and it's technology-independent. The logical data model, the LDM, is requirements analysis — it adds attributes, applies normalization, and captures business rules, and it's still technology-independent. The physical data model, the PDM, is the design activity — it's the technical solution for a specific technology, with denormalization, indexing, and partitioning, and it is technology-specific. The key relationships: conceptual and logical together are requirements work; physical is design work. And each level is technology-independent until you reach physical.

1.title: Physical Model Variants
1.text: At the physical level, the DMBOK describes several variants worth knowing. A canonical model is for data in motion between systems — think web services, an enterprise service bus, or application integration — and it's designed to be generic so it can be reused. Views are virtual tables; they simplify queries and control access, and they come in two flavors: a standard view runs its SQL at query time, while a materialized view is precomputed at a predetermined time. Partitioning splits a table — vertically, meaning you separate groups of columns, or horizontally, meaning you separate groups of rows, like regional customer tables. And denormalization is the deliberate introduction of redundancy to improve performance or enforce security; a star schema is fully denormalized. Two facts to anchor: canonical means data in motion, and vertical partitioning splits columns while horizontal splits rows.

1.title: Normalization — Purpose & Forms
1.text: Normalization is the process of organizing business complexity into stable data structures by keeping each attribute in only one place, which eliminates redundancy. There are six normal forms, climbing the staircase on screen. First normal form requires a valid primary key, atomic attributes — meaning no multi-valued fields — and the removal of repeating groups. Second normal form requires that every attribute depend on the whole primary key, not just part of it. Third normal form removes transitive dependencies, captured in the famous phrase "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key." Boyce-Codd Normal Form resolves overlapping composite candidate keys. Fourth normal form resolves multi-valued dependencies. And fifth normal form resolves join dependencies into basic pairs. The single most important fact: when someone says a "normalized model," they almost always mean third normal form. BCNF, 4NF, and 5NF occur rarely in practice.

1.title: Understanding 3NF (and Transitive Dependencies)
1.text: Let's make sure third normal form really clicks, because it's so heavily tested. The mantra is that every non-key attribute must depend on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key. The "nothing but the key" part is about transitive dependencies. A transitive dependency happens when a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, rather than directly on the primary key. For example, if an order table stores a customer ID and also the customer's city, the city really depends on the customer, not on the order — that's transitive, and 3NF removes it. One step further: Boyce-Codd Normal Form is stronger still, requiring that every determinant — every left-hand side of a dependency — be a superkey. So remember: transitive dependency means non-key depending on non-key, and that's exactly what 3NF eliminates.

1.title: Abstraction — Generalization & Specialization
1.text: Abstraction is the removal of details to broaden applicability while preserving the essential properties. Two complementary techniques implement it. Generalization groups common attributes up into a supertype entity. Specialization separates the distinguishing attributes down into subtype entities. And critically, subtyping implies inheritance — a subtype automatically inherits all the properties of its supertype. The classic example is School as a supertype, with University and High School as subtypes that inherit the common school attributes while adding their own. When you move to the physical level, you resolve this in one of two ways: subtype absorption, where the subtype attributes become nullable columns in the supertype's table, or supertype partition, where the supertype attributes are repeated into a separate table for each subtype. Supertype is general, subtype is specialized and inherits.

1.title: Activities & Engineering Directions
1.text: The DMBOK gives four data modeling activities, neatly mapped to the plan-develop-control-operate pattern: Plan for data modeling, Build the models — conceptual, logical, and physical, Review the models, and Manage the models. Then there are two engineering directions you must not confuse. Forward engineering goes from conceptual to logical to physical — CDM to LDM to PDM — and it's what you do when building a new application from requirements. Reverse engineering goes the other way, from physical to logical to conceptual — PDM to LDM to CDM — and it's what you do when documenting a database that already exists. So: forward is requirements to build, reverse is existing database to documentation.

1.title: The 8 Physical Design Steps
1.text: When you create the physical data model, the DMBOK lays out eight steps. One, resolve the logical abstractions, using subtype absorption or supertype partition. Two, add attribute details — physical names, data types, lengths, constraints, nullability. Three, add reference data objects. Four, assign surrogate keys. Five, denormalize for performance. Six, index for performance, to provide alternate access paths and avoid full table scans. Seven, partition for performance, where a date key is recommended for dimensional models. And eight, create views. The thing to notice — and a likely exam angle — is that steps five, six, and seven, denormalize, index, and partition, are all done specifically for performance. Physical design is where performance optimization happens.

1.title: Tools
1.text: There are six categories of tools that support data modeling. Data modeling tools automate the modeling tasks, do forward and reverse engineering, generate DDL, and store metadata. Lineage tools capture source structures per attribute and enable impact analysis. Data profiling tools explore the actual data content and surface quality gaps and anomalies. Metadata repositories store the descriptive information and enable metadata exchange. Data model patterns are reusable structures, ranging from elementary patterns to assembly patterns to integration patterns. And industry data models are pre-built for entire industries. Three industry-model names worth remembering for the exam: ARTS for retail, SID for communications, and ACORD for insurance.

1.title: Naming Conventions & PRISM
1.text: Two best-practice topics. First, naming conventions. The international standard is ISO 11179, the Metadata Registry standard. Logical names should use full words that are meaningful to business users; physical names use abbreviations as needed with underscores between words; and class words — like Quantity, Name, or Code — go at the end of attribute names to distinguish attributes from entities. Second, database design best practices, captured in the acronym PRISM. P is performance and ease of use. R is reusability — multiple applications can use the data. I is integrity — the data always carries valid business meaning. S is security — available only to authorized users. And M is maintainability — the cost of working with the data shouldn't exceed its value. PRISM: Performance, Reusability, Integrity, Security, Maintainability.

1.title: The Data Model Scorecard®
1.text: Steve Hoberman's Data Model Scorecard is a way to evaluate model quality, and it has ten categories totaling one hundred points. You don't need to memorize all ten, but you should know the structure and especially the top-weighted categories. Three categories are worth fifteen points each: how well the model captures the requirements, how complete the model is, and how structurally sound it is. Several categories are worth ten points each — matching the scheme, leveraging generic structures, the quality of definitions, and how well the metadata matches the data. And a few are worth five points each — naming standards, readability, and enterprise consistency. The key takeaway for the exam: the three fifteen-point categories — requirements, completeness, and structural soundness — are the most heavily weighted.

1.title: Data Model Governance
1.text: Finally, governance of the models themselves. Design quality management is about balancing short-term needs, like timely delivery, against long-term needs, like secure, recoverable, sharable, and reusable structures. Design reviews should involve a group of subject-matter experts from different backgrounds, with one person facilitating and a scribe capturing the discussion; if issues can't be resolved, the owner of the system makes the final call. And model versioning requires tracking, for every change, the why, the what and how, the when — both approved and made — the who, and the where, meaning which models were affected. One role distinction the exam may test: the data modeler defines the structure and business meaning of data, while the database administrator implements and operates the database in production.

1.title: Key Numbers & Quick Facts (Cheat Sheet)
1.text: Let's consolidate the numbers, because this chapter has many. Four building blocks. Seven entity categories. Six modeling schemes. The relational model came from Codd in 1970 with the principle "one fact in one place." Fact tables take about ninety percent of space, dimension tables about ten percent. There are three SCD types, remembered as ORC. There are six normal forms, with 3NF being the standard "normalized" form. ANSI/SPARC dates to 1975 with its three schemas. The three levels are conceptual, logical, and physical. PRISM gives you the five design principles. The scorecard has ten categories totaling one hundred points. And the naming standard is ISO 11179. Drill these until they're instant.

1.title: Common Exam Traps (Part 1)
1.text: Let me steer you around the traps, starting with four. First: don't resolve a many-to-many relationship by dumping attributes onto one side — create an associative entity to hold them. Second: "employee reports to employee" doesn't need two entities; it's a recursive, or unary, relationship on a single entity. Third: be precise about the normal forms — removing repeating groups is first normal form, while third normal form is about removing transitive dependencies; the exam will try to swap those. And fourth: surrogate keys have no business meaning and aren't visible to users, so any answer claiming a surrogate key is "self-documenting" or "business-meaningful" is wrong. Get these four straight and you'll avoid the most common modeling mistakes.

1.title: Common Exam Traps (Part 2)
1.text: Four more traps. First: a star schema has denormalized dimensions, while a snowflake has normalized dimensions — don't reverse them. Second: fact tables are not small; they take up about ninety percent of the space. Third: forward engineering goes conceptual to physical, and reverse engineering goes physical to conceptual — keep the direction straight. And fourth: Object-Role Modeling, the fact-based scheme, has no attributes; if an answer says ORM is attribute-based, it's wrong. A general tip: the phrase "one fact in one place" belongs to the relational world, while "grain" belongs to the dimensional world — don't let the exam mix those vocabularies in a single answer.

1.title: Module Summary
1.text: Let's bring it together. Data modeling discovers, analyzes, and scopes requirements into a precise data model, through an iterative journey from conceptual to logical to physical — and it's a foundation for Master Data Management and governance. There are four building blocks: entities, relationships, attributes, and domains, and you resolve many-to-many relationships with an associative entity. There are six schemes — relational with its "one fact in one place," dimensional with star and snowflake schemas, slowly changing dimensions and grain, plus object-oriented, fact-based, time-based, and NoSQL. Normalization to third normal form means "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key." And you apply PRISM, ISO 11179 naming, and the hundred-point Data Model Scorecard to ensure quality. That's the heart of Chapter 5.

1.title: Let's Test Your Knowledge
1.text: Time for five practice questions on data modeling and design. This is another heavily weighted chapter, so these points really matter. Several of these questions describe a modeling scenario and ask for the correct resolution, so read each one carefully, picture the model in your head, commit to an answer, and then reveal the solution. Let's go.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one: a many-to-many relationship between ORDER and PRODUCT carries the attributes quantity and unitprice. How do you resolve it? The answer is C — create an associative entity, ORDERLINE, to hold those relationship-specific attributes. Putting them on ORDER or PRODUCT misplaces them, and dropping the relationship loses information.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two: each employee may report to another employee who acts as a manager. Which construct? The answer is D — a recursive, self-referencing, unary relationship on the EMPLOYEE entity. Splitting into separate EMPLOYEE and MANAGER entities duplicates the entity, and subtyping treats a role as a type, which is wrong.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three: a transitive dependency, which 3NF eliminates, occurs when? The answer is C — a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute rather than directly on the primary key. That's the essence of "nothing but the key." Option A is a 2NF partial-dependency issue; B is referential integrity.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four: a key advantage of a surrogate key? The answer is B — it's a stable, system-generated identifier that stays unchanged even when the business meaning of the natural key evolves, which reduces the ripple effect on related tables. It does not add business meaning or guarantee performance. And

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: question five: why maintain conceptual, logical, and physical models rather than just the physical one? The answer is C — each level serves a distinct audience and purpose: conceptual for business scope, logical for technology-independent structure, and physical for implementation. It's about communication, not file size or regulation. That completes Module 5. You've now covered two of the four highest-weighted chapters. Next up is Module 6, Data Storage and Operations. I'll see you there.
